data.name: Express REST API Server
data.description: Node.js/Express 4 application server hosting all REST and JSON:API endpoints for products, basket, orders, payments, file operations, LLM chat, and challenge scaffolding. threats.title: [F-003] SQL injection in login query — routes/login.ts:34
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker posts to /rest/user/login with email `admin@juice-sh.op'--`; the email is concatenated into a raw sequelize.query string, the password clause is commented out, and the server issues a signed session token for the admin row.

Impact: Authentication is bypassed for any account, including admin, yielding full control over the synthetic customer data and admin functions.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-89
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
login.ts:34 builds `SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email = '${req.body.email || ''}' ...` and passes it to models.sequelize.query without replacements.
- routes/login.ts:34

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-8 juice-shop-api → juice-shop-sqlite (internal): tb-8 assumes every SQL query uses Sequelize parameterized binding; this login query interpolates request data into raw SQL.
- tb-9 juice-shop-auth → juice-shop-sqlite (internal): The credential lookup crosses into SQLite with an unparameterized email value, breaking the tb-9 binding assumption.

Business-context trace:
applied fields: sensitive assets; source: docs/security/business-context.md; sha256: 2f8408df30db4987aae261915e726239b305f96ae5ac02dc6a360c0d5835f646

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-003 (F-003)
threats.mitigation:
M-094 — Use parameterized database queries (priority P1, effort Low)
1. Replace the template string with UserModel.findOne({ where: { email, password: security.hash(password), deletedAt: null } }) or sequelize.query with `replacements`.
2. Add an API test posting email `' OR 1=1--` that asserts 401.
Verification: POST /rest/user/login {"email":"admin@juice-sh.op'--","password":"x"} returns 401.
Reference: CWE-89

threats.description:
Interpolating request-controlled text into a SQL statement lets an attacker alter the query — exfiltrating or modifying arbitrary rows, bypassing authentication, or escalating to full database control.

Risk: Critical (likelihood Critical, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-89
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- routes/search.ts:23

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-8 juice-shop-api → juice-shop-sqlite (internal): tb-8 assumes parameterized Sequelize binding for every SQL query; search interpolates the query string into raw SQL.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-004 (F-004)
threats.mitigation:
M-069 — Parameterize the product search query in routes/search.ts (priority P1, effort Low)
1. Replace the template literal in `models.sequelize.query(...)` with a named-placeholder form: `models.sequelize.query('SELECT * FROM Products WHERE ((name LIKE :q OR description LIKE :q) AND deletedAt IS NULL) ORDER BY name', { replacements: { q: '%' + criteria + '%' }, type: models.sequelize.QueryTypes.SELECT })`.
2. Remove the 200-character truncation guard; parameterized binding makes length truncation irrelevant for injection prevention.
3. Add an API test sending `q=') UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9--` and asserting the response contains only valid product rows with no injected columns.
Verification: GET /rest/products/search?q=') OR 1=1-- returns an empty result or only products matching the literal string, with no extra rows from other tables.

threats.title: [F-005] Insecure Direct Object Reference
threats.description:
A signed-in attacker puts another user's ID into the owner field of the request (req.body.UserId and the like); the query trusts it instead of the session identity, so the attacker reads or changes every other user's records — horizontal privilege escalation across all accounts.

Risk: Critical (likelihood Critical, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-639
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- routes/address.ts:11

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → juice-shop-api (internet-facing): tb-1 authorization leg requires resource references to be checked against the authenticated user; basket id is not.

Abuse-case trace:
- AC-T-101 [fully viable, verification complete] — User reads or changes data of another user or tenant; matching steps 1 (confirmed)

Business-context trace:
applied fields: sensitive assets; source: docs/security/business-context.md; sha256: 2f8408df30db4987aae261915e726239b305f96ae5ac02dc6a360c0d5835f646

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-005 (F-005)
threats.mitigation:
M-070 — Replace client-supplied UserId with session identity in all owner filters (priority P1, effort Low)
1. In routes/address.ts:11 and all routes that filter by a user identifier, replace `req.body.UserId` (and any equivalent field such as userId or ownerId) with `req.user.id` sourced from the verified JWT payload.
2. Audit every Sequelize findAll, findOne, and update call that includes a user-identity WHERE clause and confirm each uses the session-derived identity, not a value from the request body or query string.
3. Add API tests for each affected route asserting that supplying another user's ID in the request body returns only the authenticated user's records or a 403.
Verification: Authenticated as user A, GET /rest/basket/B where B is another user's basket returns 403 or an empty result regardless of what UserId is set to in the request.

threats.title: [F-006] Eval of stored username on profile page — routes/userProfile.ts:61
threats.description:
A registered user sets their username to `#{global.process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('id')}` via POST /profile (updateUserProfile.ts:38). When they load GET /profile, userProfile.ts:54-61 strips the `#{}` wrapper and passes the remainder to eval(), executing it in the server process.

Impact: Any self-registered user gains arbitrary code execution as the Node.js process, with access to the database, signing key and host filesystem.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-95
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
`username = eval(code)` evaluates the persisted username substring whenever it matches /#{(.*)}/ and usernameXssChallenge is enabled.
- routes/userProfile.ts:61

threats.title: [F-007] Mass assignment of role on user registration
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker registers via POST /api/Users with body {"email":"x@y","password":"p","role":"admin"}. The finale-generated User resource (server.ts:501-505) creates the row from all supplied attributes, and the User model accepts 'admin' as a valid role (models/user.ts:79-97), so the new account is an administrator at creation.

Impact: Any visitor self-provisions an admin account and gains administrative access to all synthetic customer data.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-915
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
finale.resource({ model: UserModel, ... }) exposes create on /api/Users with only output exclusions (password, totpSecret) and no writable-field allowlist; the registration pre-handlers (server.ts:408-422) do not strip role.
- server.ts:501

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → juice-shop-api (internet-facing): tb-1 validation leg assumes every request body is schema-validated before handler logic; the registration body is persisted with attacker-chosen role.

Abuse-case trace:

threats.title: [F-008] Hardcoded RSA JWT signing key — lib/insecurity.ts:21
threats.description:
An attacker reads the RSA private key embedded as a string literal in lib/insecurity.ts:21 from the public source repository and signs RS256 JWTs carrying any user id and role admin. Because isAuthorized() verifies against the matching public key, the forged tokens are indistinguishable from server-issued ones.

Impact: Every deployment shares the same signing key, so anyone with the source can mint valid admin and deluxe tokens and impersonate any account, exposing the synthetic user and card data the business context lists as assets.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-321
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: configuration-defect

Evidence:
`const privateKey = '[PEM PRIVATE KEY — REDACTED]...` is a source literal used by authorize() at lib/insecurity.ts:54 and deluxeToken() at line 150.
- lib/insecurity.ts:21

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → juice-shop-api (internet-facing): Tokens forged with the embedded private key satisfy the isAuthorized() RS256 check that tb-1 relies on for authentication.

Abuse-case trace:
- AC-T-005 [fully viable, verification complete] — Authentication Bypass via Exposed Secret Material; matching steps 1 (confirmed)

Business-context trace:
applied fields: sensitive assets; source: docs/security/business-context.md; sha256: 2f8408df30db4987aae261915e726239b305f96ae5ac02dc6a360c0d5835f646

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-008 (F-008)
threats.mitigation:
M-097 — Move cryptographic keys to a managed secret store (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Remove the private key literal and load it at startup from an environment-provided path or secret manager, failing closed when absent.
2. Generate a per-deployment key pair and serve only the public key.
3. Add a startup test asserting the server refuses to start without an external key and a lint/secret-scan rule that rejects PEM literals.
Verification: grep -n 'BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY' lib/insecurity.ts returns no hit, and a token signed with the old repository key is rejected with 401.
Reference: CWE-321

threats.title: [F-009] JWT Accepted Without Signature Verification
threats.description:
Decode-only flows let an attacker construct a token with any claims (admin, sub=victim, scope=*) — no key material required.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-345
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- routes/verify.ts:114

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → juice-shop-api (internet-facing): The chat route bypasses the tb-1 authentication leg: identity for tool authorization comes from a decoded, unverified token instead of isAuthorized().

threats.mitigation:
M-071 — Replace jwt.decode with jwt.verify in all authorization-adjacent paths (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Replace every call to `jwt.decode(token)` and `jws.decode(token)` that produces a payload used for identity or access decisions with `jwt.verify(token, publicKey, { algorithms: ['RS256'] })`; catch the thrown error and return 401.

3. Add a unit test that presents a token signed with an unrelated key to the decode path and asserts it results in an authentication failure rather than a usable payload.

threats.title: [F-010] Insecure JWT Verification
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker downloads the RSA public key from the browsable /encryptionkeys directory (server.ts:277-278), signs a JWT with HS256 using that public key as the HMAC secret (or sends alg none), and presents it to any route guarded by isAuthorized(). express-jwt 0.1.3 with jsonwebtoken 0.4.0 (package.json:112,132) verifies with `secret: publicKey` and no `algorithms` option, so the forged token with role admin and any victim id is accepted.

Impact: Any caller can impersonate any user including admin on every isAuthorized()/isAccounting() route, reaching the synthetic account and payment-card data declared as the component's training targets.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-347
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
isAuthorized() passes only `secret: publicKey` to express-jwt 0.1.3 with no algorithm allowlist; lib/insecurity.ts:55 likewise calls jws.verify(token, publicKey) letting the token header pick the algorithm.
- lib/insecurity.ts:52

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-1 external → juice-shop-api (internet-facing): The tb-1 authentication leg assumes isAuthorized() rejects tokens not signed with the RS256 key; the verifier here accepts attacker-chosen algorithms.

Abuse-case trace:
- AC-T-003 [fully viable, verification complete] — Privilege Escalation to Admin via JWT Algorithm Confusion; matching steps 1 (confirmed)
- AC-T-005 [fully viable, verification complete] — Authentication Bypass via Exposed Secret Material; matching steps 2 (confirmed)

applied fields: sensitive assets; source: docs/security/business-context.md; sha256: 2f8408df30db4987aae261915e726239b305f96ae5ac02dc6a360c0d5835f646

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-010 (F-010)
threats.mitigation:
M-098 — Enforce JWT signature and algorithm verification (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Upgrade express-jwt and jsonwebtoken to current major versions and configure isAuthorized() with `algorithms: ['RS256']`.
2. Replace jws.verify(token, publicKey) in verify() with jwt.verify(token, publicKey, { algorithms: ['RS256'] }).
3. Add API tests that send alg none and HS256-with-public-key tokens to /rest/basket/1 and assert 401.
Verification: curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <HS256 token signed with jwt.pub>' /rest/user/authentication-details returns 401.
Reference: CWE-347

threats.title: [F-011] Security-question password reset
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker submits POST /rest/user/reset-password with a victim email, a guessed or researched security-question answer, and a new password. The only proof of identity is the HMAC of the answer compared at resetPassword.ts:41; the 100-per-5-minute limiter is keyed on req.ip with `trust proxy` enabled (server.ts:342-346), so rotating X-Forwarded-For removes the bound on guesses.

Impact: Successful guesses take over the victim account and its synthetic personal and payment data.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-640
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
resetPassword() sets the new password after `security.hmac(answer) === data.answer` with no token sent to the account owner.
- routes/resetPassword.ts:41

Abuse-case trace:
- AC-T-103 [fully viable, verification complete] — User takes over another account; matching steps 1 (confirmed)

Business-context trace:
applied fields: sensitive assets; source: docs/security/business-context.md; sha256: 2f8408df30db4987aae261915e726239b305f96ae5ac02dc6a360c0d5835f646

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-011 (F-011)
threats.mitigation:
M-099 — Replace security-question reset with emailed token (priority P3, effort High)
1. Issue a single-use, expiring reset token delivered to the account email and require it instead of the security answer.
2. Key the limiter on the target account as well as a non-spoofable client address and disable trust proxy unless a known proxy is configured.
3. Add tests asserting reset without a valid token returns 401 and that varying X-Forwarded-For does not reset the limit.
Verification: POST /rest/user/reset-password with correct answer but no reset token returns 401.
Reference: CWE-640

threats.title: [F-013] Plaintext TOTP secret storage — models/user.ts:112
threats.description:
An attacker who reads the Users table through any query-level flaw in the API copies a victim's totpSecret column, which is stored as a plain STRING, and generates valid second-factor codes to complete login as that user.

Impact: Disclosure of the stored seed defeats two-factor authentication for every enrolled account, letting the attacker impersonate users of the training shop including privileged ones.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-522
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
The User model declares totpSecret as a plain DataTypes.STRING column with no setter, encryption, or hashing, so the TOTP seed is persisted verbatim in data/juiceshop.sqlite.
- models/user.ts:112

threats.mitigation:
M-101 — Encrypt TOTP secrets (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Add a setter/getter pair on totpSecret that encrypts with an authenticated cipher (AES-256-GCM) using a key loaded from external secret configuration, and decrypt only inside the 2FA verification path.

threats.title: [F-015] Zip Slip path traversal in complaint upload — routes/fileUpload.ts:34
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker uploads a ZIP to POST /file-upload (no authentication, server.ts:309) containing an entry named `../../ftp/legal.md` or `../../frontend/dist/frontend/main.js`. extractZipBuffer resolves the entry path and only checks that it contains the application root (fileUpload.ts:33), so the file is written anywhere inside the application directory.

Impact: Attackers overwrite served frontend assets, FTP documents, or i18n files (autoReload at server.ts:303), defacing the shop or planting script served to every user.

Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

`fs.createWriteStream('uploads/complaints/' + fileName)` writes entry.path unsanitized; the guard `absolutePath.includes(path.resolve('.'))` permits traversal out of uploads/complaints.

threats.title: [F-031] ReDoS in SVG verify event regex — registerWebsocketEvents.ts:46
threats.description:
While the SVG injection challenge is unsolved, an anonymous attacker emits 'verifySvgInjectionChallenge' with a long string lacking the '../../..' marker; the unanchored /.*\.\.\/.../ pattern backtracks super-linearly on the main event loop, stalling the whole Node process for every user.

Impact: A single anonymous client can make the shop's API, frontend, and socket channel unresponsive for all users of the instance.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-1333
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 46 runs data?.match with an unanchored leading .* on unbounded client data; a local timing of this exact regex took 147 ms at 10k, 654 ms at 20k, and 3182 ms at 40k characters, far below the default 1 MB Socket.IO message limit.
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:46

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-2 external → juice-shop-realtime (internet-facing): The socket event payload is matched against a backtracking regex without type or length checks, breaking tb-2's validation leg.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-031 (F-031)

M-114 — Bound input and remove backtracking (priority P1, effort Low)
1. Reject non-string data and strings longer than 2048 characters before matching, and replace the regex with an anchored, non-backtracking check (for example, parse with new URL() and compare pathname and the 'to' query parameter).
2. Add a unit test that feeds a 1 MB string to the handler predicate and asserts it returns in under 50 ms.
Verification: Run `node -e "const t=Date.now();predicate('a'.repeat(1e6));console.log(Date.now()-t)"` against the extracted predicate; expected output below 50.

threats.title: [F-020] Lockfile disabled; builds resolve npm graph fresh — .npmrc:1
threats.description:
An attacker who takes over any maintainer account in Juice Shop's transitive npm graph publishes a malicious patch release; because .npmrc:1 sets package-lock=false and package-lock.json is gitignored, the next Docker build runs `npm install --omit=dev` (Dockerfile:5) against live registry state, executes the package's lifecycle scripts, and bakes the payload into bkimminich/juice-shop:latest pushed at ci.yml:338.

Impact: Arbitrary code runs in the image build and on CI runners, and a trojanized Docker image and release archives reach the security practitioners worldwide who pull the public training artifact; the declared harm of a compromised public image is directly reachable.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-829
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
.npmrc:1 contains `package-lock=false`; no package-lock.json exists in the repo (gitignored at .gitignore:10), so Dockerfile:5, ci.yml:51/71/110/147/203/238/292 and release.yml:55 all run `npm install` with semver ranges and lifecycle scripts enabled; Dockerfile:4 and :19 add ranged global installs (typescript@^6.0.3, cyclonedx-npm ^2||^3||^4). The controls claim of `npm ci` at ci.yml:36,51 is false: both lines run `npm install`.
- .npmrc:1

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-5 external → juice-shop-cicd (internet-facing): tb-5 assumes npm ci with exact lockfile versions; .npmrc disables lockfile creation so every npm install crossing the registry boundary resolves fresh.

Business-context trace:
applied fields: impact if compromised, sensitive assets; source: docs/security/business-context.md; sha256: 2f8408df30db4987aae261915e726239b305f96ae5ac02dc6a360c0d5835f646

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-020 (F-020)
threats.mitigation:
M-104 — Commit lockfiles and install from them (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Remove `package-lock=false` from .npmrc, drop package-lock.json from .gitignore and frontend/.gitignore, and commit both generated lockfiles.
2. Replace `npm install` with `npm ci` in Dockerfile:5, ci.yml and release.yml, and change the postinstall frontend install (package.json:56) to `npm ci`.
3. Pin global tool installs (Dockerfile:4, Dockerfile:19, ci.yml:282-284) to exact versions and add a CI check that fails when the lockfile is missing or out of sync.
Verification: Run `test -f package-lock.json && test -f frontend/package-lock.json && ! grep -q 'package-lock=false' .npmrc && ! grep -nE 'npm install( |$)(--omit|--production|$)' Dockerfile .github/workflows/ci.yml .github/workflows/release.yml`; expected exit code 0.

threats.title: [F-045] Base images referenced by floating tag, no digest
threats.description:
An attacker who can publish to the node:24 tag or the gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13 tag (or poison a registry mirror) substitutes a backdoored image; the next CI build at ci.yml:338 uses it as installer and runtime base and pushes the result as bkimminich/juice-shop.

Impact: A substituted base layer ships inside the public training image and runs under every consumer's container runtime.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-1357
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Dockerfile:1 `FROM node:24 AS installer` and Dockerfile:22 `FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13` carry no `@sha256:` digest, so each build pulls whatever the tag currently points to.
- Dockerfile:1

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-4 external → juice-shop-cicd (internet-facing): tb-4 assumes every base image is referenced by digest; Dockerfile:1 uses the floating node:24 tag.

Business-context trace:

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-045 (F-045)
threats.mitigation:
M-124 — Set least-privilege CI workflow permissions (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Change Dockerfile:1 and Dockerfile:22 to `image:tag@sha256:<digest>` and let Dependabot/Renovate (docker ecosystem) raise digest-update PRs.
2. Add a build check that rejects FROM lines without a digest.
Verification: Run `grep -nE '^FROM ' Dockerfile | grep -v '@sha256:'`; expected no output.
Reference: CWE-1357

threats.description:

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-250
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: config-scan

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-058 (F-058)
threats.mitigation:
M-080 — Add USER <non-root-uid> to test/smoke/Dockerfile (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Add a non-root user to test/smoke/Dockerfile before the CMD directive: `RUN addgroup -S smoke && adduser -S smoke -G smoke` followed by `USER smoke`.
2. Verify the smoke test commands inside the container do not require root-level filesystem access; adjust file permissions or volume mounts if the test runner cannot write to its working directory as the non-root user.
Verification: grep -E '^USER ' test/smoke/Dockerfile; expected at least one match with a non-root user.

threats.title: [F-059] Missing Workflow Permissions Block
threats.description:
Missing Workflow Permissions Block: Without an explicit permissions block at workflow or job level, the job inherits the repository default (commonly write-all) for GITHUB_TOKEN — any compromised step can push code, create releases, or approve PRs.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-732
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: config-scan

Evidence:
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:25

Business-context trace:
applied fields: impact if compromised, sensitive assets; source: docs/security/business-context.md; sha256: 2f8408df30db4987aae261915e726239b305f96ae5ac02dc6a360c0d5835f646

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-059 (F-059)
threats.mitigation:
M-081 — Add `permissions: contents: read` at workflow root; elevate per-job only where needed (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Add a top-level `permissions: contents: read` block to ci.yml between the `env:` and `jobs:` keys; grant elevated permissions (`contents: write`, `packages: write`, `pull-requests: write`) only on the individual jobs that push Docker images, create releases, or open pull requests.
2. Repeat for image_actions.yml and lint-fixer.yml: add top-level `permissions: contents: read`, with per-job elevation only on the auto-commit job in lint-fixer and the PR-creation job in image_actions.
Verification: grep -E '^permissions:' .github/workflows/ci.yml .github/workflows/image_actions.yml .github/workflows/lint-fixer.yml; expected one match per file.

threats.title: [F-063] Workflows lack permissions block; token persisted — ci.yml:25
threats.description:
An attacker whose malicious npm release is pulled by `npm install` (ci.yml:51, with the nested postinstall install at package.json:56) on a push build reads the GITHUB_TOKEN that actions/checkout persisted in .git/config; because ci.yml declares no `permissions:` block the token carries the repository default scope, which lint-fixer.yml and image_actions.yml show includes contents write, so the attacker pushes commits to the repository.

Impact: A compromised dependency or action escalates from build-step code execution to repository write, letting it tamper with source that ships in the public Docker image.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-250
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
ci.yml, image_actions.yml and lint-fixer.yml contain zero `permissions:` keys and zero `persist-credentials` overrides; lint-fixer.yml:22 auto-commits and image_actions.yml:42 creates PRs with the default token, which proves the repository default grants contents write. ci.yml jobs run install scripts after checkout (ci.yml:51, 71, 110, 147, 203, 238).
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:25

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-3 external → juice-shop-cicd (internet-facing): tb-3 assumes GITHUB_TOKEN permissions are scoped per job; ci.yml declares no permissions block so jobs inherit the write-capable default.

Business-context trace:
applied fields: impact if compromised, sensitive assets; source: docs/security/business-context.md; sha256: 2f8408df30db4987aae261915e726239b305f96ae5ac02dc6a360c0d5835f646

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-063 (F-063)
threats.mitigation:
M-139 — Drop unnecessary privileges in build and runtime (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Add top-level `permissions: contents: read` to ci.yml, image_actions.yml and lint-fixer.yml, granting `contents: write`/`pull-requests: write` only on the jobs that commit or open PRs.
2. Set `persist-credentials: false` on every actions/checkout step whose job does not push.
3. Run install steps with `--ignore-scripts` where tests do not need lifecycle scripts.
Verification: Run `for f in .github/workflows/ci.yml .github/workflows/image_actions.yml .github/workflows/lint-fixer.yml; do grep -q '^permissions:' $f || echo MISSING $f; done`; expected no output.
Reference: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/security-guides/automatic-token-authentication#modifying-the-permissions-for-the-github_token
